screens.title: Estimating Scale: Throughput, Storage & Latency
screens.narratorSegment: In system design, good architecture begins with a few quick, honest estimates. We call these back-of-the-envelope calculations. They are not precise billing numbers; they are order-of-magnitude checks that tell you whether a single server will suffice or whether you need a globally distributed fleet. On this lesson board you will learn how to estimate requests per second from user signals, how to translate item sizes into gigabytes or petabytes, how to convert RPS into bandwidth needs, and how to use common latency numbers to reason about caching and data locality. We will use concrete examples — like a photo-sharing service — and we will always state assumptions. That practice of naming assumptions is as important as the arithmetic itself. By the end you will be able to perform quick RPS calculations, project storage growth for years, and compare memory, disk, and network latency to make pragmatic design choices. Keep a notebook handy: these are skills you will repeat many times in interviews and in real designs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Estimating Scale
Estimating Scale: Throughput, Storage & Latency
Practical back-of-the-envelope methods used to guide early architecture decisions.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Throughput
Estimate RPS from DAU and actions/day, then multiply by peak factor.
Storage
Multiply item size by item count, include metadata, indexes, and replication.
Latency
Compare memory, disk, and network latencies to plan caching and locality.
In this lesson

You will compute average and peak RPS, estimate storage growth for photos, convert RPS to bandwidth, and use latency numbers to justify caches.

Coming up

A step-by-step photo service example, practical assumptions, and common mistakes to avoid.

Key Idea

Order-of-magnitude reasoning and explicit assumptions save time and reduce costly design errors.

Visual Quick Reference
Throughput Example
100M DAU × 10 actions/day ≈ 11,574 RPS avg
Storage Example
100M profiles × 1KB = 100 GB; photos grow to PBs with large user bases.
Latency Reference
Memory ~100 ns; SSD read ~150 µs; cross-continental ~150 ms.
Use these as starting points. Always state assumptions and round to an order of magnitude.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills. First, you will perform back-of-the-envelope throughput calculations from user behavior. That matters because interviews and early design stages require fast judgments about scale. For a concrete example, we'll compute RPS from DAU and actions per user. Second, you will estimate storage needs for profiles, photos, and replicas. This helps you decide between a single large disk or distributed object storage. You will practice multiplying item size by item count and including metadata and replication. Third, you will convert load into bandwidth requirements and learn to reason about CDN placement and egress costs. You will see how RPS times payload size becomes bytes per second and how to compare that against typical link capacities. Fourth, you will recall and use typical latency numbers — memory, SSD, disk, and international round trips — to justify caches and data locality. For each objective you'll state assumptions, round to an order of magnitude, and explain the practical implication of the estimate.

screens.title: How to think when estimating
screens.narratorSegment: Good estimates begin with explicit assumptions. State the user counts, actions per user per day, average payload sizes, and expected read-to-write ratio. Next, round values to an order of magnitude where useful: 1.3 billion becomes 1 billion when you only need scale. Third, always compute both average and peak: average RPS gives baseline cost; peak RPS drives capacity planning. Fourth, include replication and metadata when estimating storage, and include CDN and egress paths when calculating bandwidth. Finally, treat latency numbers as rules of thumb: you will use memory and network latency comparisons to justify caches and local replicas. As a concrete example, assume 100 million DAU, 10 actions per day, and a 5x peak factor to immediately see whether one region can handle bursts or whether you need global distribution. This mental checklist will become your default interview script: state assumptions, show arithmetic, explain why you rounded, and finish with the implication for architecture and trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › How to think
How to think when estimating
A reproducible checklist for interview-grade estimates.
Checklist
  • State user counts, actions/day, and payload sizes.
  • Round to order of magnitude when exactness is unnecessary.
  • Compute average RPS and apply a peak multiplier.
  • Include metadata, indexes, and replication in storage.
  • Compare latency numbers to justify caching and locality.
Concrete example
Assume 100M DAU, 10 actions/day → 1B actions/day. Average RPS ≈ 1B/86,400 ≈ 11,574. If peak is 5x, plan for ~58k RPS. State each assumption and round to tidy numbers when presenting.
Assumption: DAU and actions per DAU
Rounding: Order-of-magnitude
Peak factor: 2–10×
Key Takeaway

A short, stated assumption list and order-of-magnitude arithmetic are often the most persuasive parts of a system design answer.

screens.title: Estimating Throughput (RPS/QPS)
screens.narratorSegment: Throughput estimation begins by converting user activity into requests per second. Start with a clear assumption: how many Daily Active Users does your system have, and how many actions does each perform per day? Multiply those two numbers to get total actions per day. Then divide by the number of seconds in a day, 86,400, to produce an average RPS. This average helps estimate baseline capacity and cost. But traffic isn't uniform. Apply a peak multiplier — commonly between two and ten — to model busy periods. For example, if you assume 100 million DAU and 10 actions per DAU, you get one billion actions per day. Dividing by 86,400 yields about 11,574 RPS average. If you expect a 5× peak, plan for roughly 57,870 RPS. Also consider read-to-write mix: if 90% of those actions are reads, most capacity should favor read scaling and caching. A common misconception is over-optimizing for average RPS; peak capacity, not average, usually determines the number of front-end instances and cache size. Practice this calculation with different peak factors and user assumptions to see how architecture needs shift.

keyIdea.title: Throughput formula
keyIdea.text: Total actions/day ÷ 86,400 = average RPS. Multiply by peak factor (2–10×) for capacity planning.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Throughput
Process: Compute RPS
A short, repeatable calculation you'll use often.
Step 1: Count actions/day
DAU × actions per DAU → total actions/day.
Step 2: Convert to average RPS
Average RPS = total actions/day ÷ 86,400 seconds.
Step 3: Apply peak factor
Multiply average RPS by expected peak multiplier (2–10×).
Concrete calculation
100,000,000 DAU × 10 actions/day = 1,000,000,000 actions/day
Average RPS = 1,000,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 11,574 RPS
Peak RPS (5×) ≈ 11,574 × 5 ≈ 57,870 RPS
Explanation and guidance
  • Average RPS helps estimate cost; peak RPS drives capacity decisions like load balancers and autoscaling thresholds.
  • Adjust the peak multiplier for day/night cycles, promotions, or sudden viral spikes.
  • Remember read-heavy systems benefit more from caching; write-heavy systems need strong storage and replication plans.
Key Takeaway

Compute average RPS first, then inflate it with a peak factor. Use the peak value to size front-end and cache capacity.

Common Mistake
Planning only for average RPS and ignoring peak bursts leads to outages under load.

screens.title: Read-to-Write Ratio and Its Impact
screens.narratorSegment: The read-to-write ratio describes the proportion of read operations to write operations in your workload. This single number often dictates major architectural choices. For example, if 90% of operations are reads and only 10% are writes, you should prioritize read scalability: large, distributed caches, read replicas for databases, and aggressive content delivery networks. Reads can be served from caches far more cheaply and at lower latency than writes. Writes are typically more expensive because they require durability and stronger consistency, so you must plan storage, replication, and write throughput. A common misconception is assuming reads and writes are equally easy to scale; they are not. Reads are usually scale-out friendly, while writes often require sharding, batching, or asynchronous replication. As a concrete scenario, if your photo service has a 10:1 read-to-write ratio for photos and peak photo reads are high, a combination of CDN edge caches plus origin read replicas will dramatically reduce origin load. Always state the ratio when you present throughput or storage estimates, because it changes where you place cost and complexity. Read-to-Write Ratio and Its Impact means high read ratios favor caching and cdns; high write ratios require sharding, durable storage, and careful replication.. In practical terms, why read-heavy systems need different solutions than write-heavy ones. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Read-to-Write Ratio
What the read-to-write ratio means
A single number that changes caching, replication, and storage strategy.
Read-heavy (e.g., 90:10)
Favor caches, CDNs, and many read replicas. Reduce origin load and latency for users.
Write-heavy
Plan for sharding, batching, and durable storage with replication and stronger consistency models.
Concrete scenario
Photo service: read-to-write ratio 10:1. If peak reads are high, put photos on CDN edges so origin storage handles writes and background replication only.
Visual: Impact map
Scaling focus
Reads → Cache & replicas. Writes → Storage and consistency.
Operational trade-off
More read replicas lower latency but increase operational complexity and replication lag risk.
Common mistake
Treating writes as cheap to scale; this underestimates storage throughput and durability needs.
Key Takeaway

Always include the read-to-write ratio in throughput and architecture estimates — it changes the solution.

screens.title: From User Actions to Bandwidth
screens.narratorSegment: After you know RPS, the next step is to estimate bandwidth. Bandwidth planning is simply multiplication: RPS times average payload size produces bytes per second. Convert payload sizes into bytes consistently and remember whether measurements are bytes or bits — a common pitfall is mixing the two. For example, if peak RPS is 57,870 and each response transfers 1 KB, then outgoing bandwidth is 57,870 KB/s, which is about 57.87 MB/s. If you need bits per second for link comparison, multiply bytes by eight. In practice you will also account for headers, TLS overhead, and internal service traffic. A useful example: serving 1 MB photo reads at 10,000 RPS is extreme and would imply tens of gigabits per second. Use CDNs to push static payloads near users and reduce origin bandwidth. The mental checklist is: calculate RPS, estimate payload size after compression, multiply, and convert to the units of the network links you will use. Always sanity-check the result against typical link capacities like 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, or higher. From User Actions to Bandwidth means bandwidth (b/s) = rps × average payload size (bytes). convert to bits/s by ×8 and compare to link capacity.. In practical terms, turn rps and payload sizes into bytes-per-second for network planning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bandwidth rule
keyIdea.text: Bandwidth (B/s) = RPS × average payload size (bytes). Convert to bits/s by ×8 and compare to link capacity.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Bandwidth
Top/bottom: Calculation + example
Convert RPS × payload → B/s, then to bits/s for link sizing.
Peak RPS = 57,870
Payload = 1 KB = 1,024 bytes
Bandwidth = 57,870 × 1,024 ≈ 59,276,880 bytes/s ≈ 59.28 MB/s
Bits/s = 59,276,880 × 8 ≈ 474,215,040 bits/s ≈ 474.2 Mbps
Note: using 1 KB ≈ 1,000 bytes simplifies numbers. Always state which conversion you use. Add 10–30% overhead for TLS and headers if you are budgeting network capacity.
Practical guidance
  • For large static payloads like photos and videos, prefer CDN edges to reduce origin egress.
  • Compare computed bits/s to available link speeds (1 Gbps = 1,000 Mbps roughly) and budget headroom.
  • Account for internal service-to-service traffic separately; it can be significant at scale.
Key Takeaway

RPS × payload gives bytes per second. Convert to bits per second for link capacity and plan CDNs for large static content.

screens.title: Storage Estimation: Profiles vs Media
screens.narratorSegment: Storage estimation requires separating small, frequent items from large, infrequent ones. User profile records are compact — often a few kilobytes — while media like photos or videos are megabytes each. Multiply item size by item count to estimate raw storage. For example, if each profile is 1 KB and you have 100 million users, that's about 100 GB of raw profile data. Contrast that with photos: if every user uploads 10 photos per year at 2 MB each and there are 100 million users, yearly photo additions are 2,000 TB or about 2 PB. Always include metadata, thumbnails, indexes, and replication factors. If you keep three replicas for durability, multiply your raw totals by three. A frequent error is forgetting these multipliers and underestimating storage by factors of two or three. Also plan for growth: project annual additions and cumulative totals over multi-year horizons. Finally, mention compression assumptions explicitly, for instance saying '2 MB after compression', because swapping that number will change storage estimates drastically. Storage Estimation: Profiles vs Media means storage = sum(item_size × item_count) across data types, plus metadata, indexes, and replication factors.. In practical terms, how small profile records and large media files combine to shape storage needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Storage Estimation
Top: Compare small records and large media
Profiles are small; media is large — both matter differently.
Profile example
100,000,000 users × 1 KB = 100,000,000 KB ≈ 100 GB
Photo growth example
100,000,000 users × 10 photos/user/year × 2 MB/photo = 2,000,000,000 MB/year = 2,000 TB/year = 2 PB/year
Practical considerations
  • Include thumbnails, metadata, and index overhead as an additional 10–50% depending on schema.
  • Apply replication factor for durability; three replicas triple raw totals.
  • Project cumulative totals across years to see when distributed storage becomes necessary.
Key Takeaway

Small records add up, but media files drive petabyte-scale storage. Always state compression and replication assumptions.

Common Mistake
Forgetting replication or metadata margins underestimates storage needs by large factors.

screens.title: Design implications of storage scale
screens.narratorSegment: When raw storage numbers reach hundreds of terabytes or petabytes, a single server or a small cluster is no longer realistic. This forces a move to distributed object storage, sharded databases, or cloud-managed blob stores. The decision threshold depends on durability needs, access patterns, and budget. If reads are frequent for recent items, you might add a cache or a hot store for recent objects and place cold data in cheaper, distributed object storage. Replication and geographic distribution add further costs and complexity but are necessary for availability. For instance, a system with 2 PB of photo uploads per year should architect for multi-node, distributed storage and lifecycle policies like tiering to colder, cheaper storage after 6–12 months. Also plan operational activities: data rebalancing, snapshotting, and backup windows become non-trivial at this scale. Misconceptions include underestimating the operational effort of petabyte-scale storage and assuming simply adding disks to one machine will scale. At scale, consider object stores, erasure coding, and cross-region replication strategies. Design implications of storage scale means hundreds of tb to pbs require distributed storage, tiering strategies, and significant operational planning.. In practical terms, when to move from single-node to distributed object storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: When to distribute
keyIdea.text: Hundreds of TB to PBs require distributed storage, tiering strategies, and significant operational planning.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Storage Architecture
When scale demands distributed storage
Operational costs, durability, and access patterns drive architecture.
Tiering
Keep hot data on fast stores; move cold data to cheaper object storage with lifecycle policies.
Replication & durability
Use replication or erasure coding. Factor these into storage estimates and recovery planning.
Operational tasks
Rebalancing, backups, and migrations become large projects at petabyte scale.
Concrete architecture pattern
Use CDN + hot store + cold blob store. Writes go to origin; frequently-read items cached at edge. Background jobs tier older objects to cheaper storage classes.
Key Takeaway

At TB–PB scale, design for tiering, replication, and operational workflows rather than relying on single-node expansions.

screens.title: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know
screens.narratorSegment: Latency differences dictate whether you cache, colocate, or accept asynchronous behavior. Here are a set of reference numbers to keep in your head: L1 cache reference is sub-nanosecond; main memory reads are on the order of 100 nanoseconds; compressing 1 KB might take a few microseconds; sending 1 KB over a 1 Gbps link is about 10 microseconds; random 4 KB SSD reads are roughly 150 microseconds; a round trip inside a datacenter is around 500 microseconds; reading 1 MB sequentially from an SSD is about one millisecond; a disk seek is about 10 milliseconds; a round trip between continents can be on the order of 150 milliseconds. These are rules of thumb rather than exact benchmarks, but they show how many orders of magnitude separate memory, storage, and network. Use these numbers to justify cache placement: if a remote call costs 100 ms but memory access is 0.1 µs, caching can reduce user-visible latency by orders of magnitude. A common mistake is treating all input and output as similar; they are not — plan accordingly. Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know means memory, ssd, disk, and network latencies differ by several orders of magnitude and should drive caching and replication decisions.. In practical terms, order-of-magnitude reference times from cache to cross-continent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Use these numbers to justify cache placement: if a remote call costs 100 ms but memory access is 0.1 µs, caching can reduce user-visible latency by orders of magnitude. A common mistake is treating all input and output as similar; they are not — plan accordingly. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Latency Numbers
Latency benchmarks
Order-of-magnitude times to keep in mind when designing systems.
  • L1 cache reference: ~0.5 ns
  • Branch mispredict: ~5 ns
  • L2 cache reference: ~7 ns
  • Mutex lock/unlock: ~25 ns
  • Main memory reference: ~100 ns
  • Compress 1K bytes: ~3,000 ns (3 µs)
  • Send 1K bytes over 1 Gbps: ~10,000 ns (10 µs)
  • Read 4K random from SSD: ~150,000 ns (150 µs)
  • Round trip within datacenter: ~500,000 ns (0.5 ms)
  • Read 1 MB sequential from SSD: ~1,000,000 ns (1 ms)
  • Disk seek: ~10,000,000 ns (10 ms)
  • Round trip America–Europe: ~150,000,000 ns (150 ms)
Use these numbers to decide whether to cache, replicate, or accept remote calls. If a remote call is 150 ms, but a cache hit is a few hundred nanoseconds, caching dramatically improves user latency and overall throughput.
Key Takeaway

Orders of magnitude separate memory, disk, and network. These differences determine whether to cache or colocate data.

keyIdea.text: Compute uploads from DAU and uploads/day. Use read ratio to get reads and apply peak factor for capacity planning.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Photo-sharing Example
Step-by-step arithmetic
Compute uploads and reads from DAU and ratios.
Given:
Total users = 500,000,000
DAU = 100,000,000
Uploads per DAU per day = 2
Photo size = 1 MB
Read-to-write ratio = 10:1
Peak factor = 4x

Uploads/day = 100,000,000 × 2 = 200,000,000
Average upload RPS = 200,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 2,314 RPS
Peak upload RPS = 2,314 × 4 ≈ 9,256 RPS

Photo reads/day = uploads/day × 10 = 2,000,000,000
Average read RPS = 2,000,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 23,148 RPS
Peak read RPS = 23,148 × 4 ≈ 92,592 RPS
Implications
  • Reads dominate traffic: plan CDN and cache capacity for ~100k peak RPS on reads.
  • Uploads are smaller in RPS but require durable storage throughput for writes and replication.
  • State your assumptions about compression and read patterns when presenting estimates.
Key Takeaway

Separate upload and read calculations. Reads often determine CDN and cache sizing; writes determine storage throughput.

screens.narratorSegment: Continuing the photo-sharing example, use earlier counts to estimate storage and bandwidth. If every DAU uploads 2 photos/day, that was 200 million uploads per day. Over five years, and assuming every user eventually uploads at the given rate, total photos are: 500 million users × 10 photos/year × 5 years = 25 billion photos. keyIdea.text: Multi-year media retention leads to PB scale. Peak read bandwidth for MB payloads can reach hundreds of Gbps — CDNs are essential.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Photo-sharing Storage & Bandwidth
Storage projection (5 years)
Show cumulative growth and replication impact.
Total users = 500,000,000
Photos per user per year = 10
Years = 5
Total photos = 500,000,000 × 10 × 5 = 25,000,000,000 photos
At 1 MB/photo → 25,000,000,000 MB ≈ 24,414 TB ≈ 23.8 PB (raw)
With 3× replication ≈ 71.4 PB
State whether photos are retained indefinitely. If you archive older photos to cold storage, you can delay or reduce the hot storage footprint and related costs.
Outgoing bandwidth for reads
Use peak read RPS and payload size to compute bits per second.
Peak read RPS ≈ 92,592
Payload = 1 MB
Bandwidth ≈ 92,592 MB/s ≈ 92.592 GB/s
Bits/s ≈ 92.592 × 8 ≈ 740.7 Gbps
At this scale, CDN edges and regional caches are necessary to avoid multi-hundred-gigabit origin links and runaway costs.
Key Takeaway

Large-scale media retention and MB-sized payloads quickly drive bandwidth to hundreds of gigabits. CDNs and tiering are not optional at that scale.

screens.title: Unit conversions and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Unit conversion errors are one of the most common mistakes during estimation. Always track whether your sizes are in bytes or bits. Network link capacities are often quoted in bits per second (for example, 1 Gbps), while payload sizes are usually measured in bytes. Remember: 1 byte = 8 bits. Also be careful with kilo versus kibibyte conventions; using 1,000 vs 1,024 changes numbers but usually not the order of magnitude. Time units matter too: convert days to seconds (86,400) to compute RPS. Another frequent omission is replication: when you plan for three replicas for durability, multiply raw storage by three. Finally, account for headers, protocol overhead, and non-payload bytes in network calculations. A simple checklist fixes many errors: annotate units next to every number, convert early, round to a comfortable figure, and state replication and compression assumptions. If you present estimates this way, reviewers can follow your logic and spot faulty assumptions quickly. In practical terms, bytes vs bits, seconds vs milliseconds, and replication multipliers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Unit Conversions
Checklist for unit safety
Annotate units, convert early, and include overheads.
Bytes vs bits
Payload in bytes × 8 → bits for network links in bps.
Seconds conversion
Days → seconds = 86,400. Use this for requests/day to RPS conversions.
Replication and overhead
Multiply raw storage for replicas and add 10–30% for headers and metadata.
Example pitfall
If you compute 57.87 MB/s and compare to a 1 Gbps link without multiplying by 8, you will under-provision and misrepresent required capacity. Always convert to the same unit family before comparing.
Key Takeaway

Unit errors are low-hanging mistakes. Annotate units and convert early to avoid them.

screens.title: Practice: Rapid estimation checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When asked an estimation question in an interview or design meeting, follow a short script: first, state your assumptions clearly — DAU, actions per user, payload sizes, read/write ratio, and peak factor. Second, compute total actions/day and convert to average RPS by dividing by 86,400. Third, apply your peak multiplier and separate reads and writes using your ratio. Fourth, compute storage per data type (profiles, media) and multiply by replication. Fifth, compute bandwidth by multiplying peak RPS by payload size and converting to bits per second. Sixth, use latency reference numbers to justify caching and replication choices. Finally, sanity-check results against typical link sizes and known thresholds: is the resulting bandwidth tens of Mbps, hundreds of Mbps, or hundreds of Gbps? State the implication: CDN necessary, single region sufficient, or multi-region needed. This script keeps you organized, helps interviewers follow your logic, and makes clear where estimations could swing based on assumptions. Try it aloud when practicing. fullNarratorScript:
In system design, good architecture begins with a few quick, honest estimates. We call these back-of-the-envelope calculations. They are not precise billing numbers; they are order-of-magnitude checks that tell you whether a single server will suffice or whether you need a globally distributed fleet. On this lesson board you will learn how to estimate requests per second from user signals, how to translate item sizes into gigabytes or petabytes, how to convert RPS into bandwidth needs, and how to use common latency numbers to reason about caching and data locality. We will use concrete examples — like a photo-sharing service — and we will always state assumptions. That practice of naming assumptions is as important as the arithmetic itself. By the end you will be able to perform quick RPS calculations, project storage growth for years, and compare memory, disk, and network latency to make pragmatic design choices. Keep a notebook handy: these are skills you will repeat many times in interviews and in real designs.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills. First, you will perform back-of-the-envelope throughput calculations from user behavior. That matters because interviews and early design stages require fast judgments about scale. For a concrete example, we'll compute RPS from DAU and actions per user. Second, you will estimate storage needs for profiles, photos, and replicas. This helps you decide between a single large disk or distributed object storage. You will practice multiplying item size by item count and including metadata and replication. Third, you will convert load into bandwidth requirements and learn to reason about CDN placement and egress costs. You will see how RPS times payload size becomes bytes per second and how to compare that against typical link capacities. Fourth, you will recall and use typical latency numbers — memory, SSD, disk, and international round trips — to justify caches and data locality. For each objective you'll state assumptions, round to an order of magnitude, and explain the practical implication of the estimate.

Good estimates begin with explicit assumptions. State the user counts, actions per user per day, average payload sizes, and expected read-to-write ratio. Next, round values to an order of magnitude where useful: 1.3 billion becomes 1 billion when you only need scale. Third, always compute both average and peak: average RPS gives baseline cost; peak RPS drives capacity planning. Fourth, include replication and metadata when estimating storage, and include CDN and egress paths when calculating bandwidth. Finally, treat latency numbers as rules of thumb: you will use memory and network latency comparisons to justify caches and local replicas. As a concrete example, assume 100 million DAU, 10 actions per day, and a 5x peak factor to immediately see whether one region can handle bursts or whether you need global distribution. This mental checklist will become your default interview script: state assumptions, show arithmetic, explain why you rounded, and finish with the implication for architecture and trade-offs.

Throughput estimation begins by converting user activity into requests per second. Start with a clear assumption: how many Daily Active Users does your system have, and how many actions does each perform per day? Multiply those two numbers to get total actions per day. Then divide by the number of seconds in a day, 86,400, to produce an average RPS. This average helps estimate baseline capacity and cost. But traffic isn't uniform. Apply a peak multiplier — commonly between two and ten — to model busy periods. For example, if you assume 100 million DAU and 10 actions per DAU, you get one billion actions per day. Dividing by 86,400 yields about 11,574 RPS average. If you expect a 5× peak, plan for roughly 57,870 RPS. Also consider read-to-write mix: if 90% of those actions are reads, most capacity should favor read scaling and caching. A common misconception is over-optimizing for average RPS; peak capacity, not average, usually determines the number of front-end instances and cache size. Practice this calculation with different peak factors and user assumptions to see how architecture needs shift.

The read-to-write ratio describes the proportion of read operations to write operations in your workload. This single number often dictates major architectural choices. For example, if 90% of operations are reads and only 10% are writes, you should prioritize read scalability: large, distributed caches, read replicas for databases, and aggressive content delivery networks. Reads can be served from caches far more cheaply and at lower latency than writes. Writes are typically more expensive because they require durability and stronger consistency, so you must plan storage, replication, and write throughput. A common misconception is assuming reads and writes are equally easy to scale; they are not. Reads are usually scale-out friendly, while writes often require sharding, batching, or asynchronous replication. As a concrete scenario, if your photo service has a 10:1 read-to-write ratio for photos and peak photo reads are high, a combination of CDN edge caches plus origin read replicas will dramatically reduce origin load. Always state the ratio when you present throughput or storage estimates, because it changes where you place cost and complexity. Read-to-Write Ratio and Its Impact means high read ratios favor caching and cdns; high write ratios require sharding, durable storage, and careful replication.. In practical terms, why read-heavy systems need different solutions than write-heavy ones. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After you know RPS, the next step is to estimate bandwidth. Bandwidth planning is simply multiplication: RPS times average payload size produces bytes per second. Convert payload sizes into bytes consistently and remember whether measurements are bytes or bits — a common pitfall is mixing the two. For example, if peak RPS is 57,870 and each response transfers 1 KB, then outgoing bandwidth is 57,870 KB/s, which is about 57.87 MB/s. If you need bits per second for link comparison, multiply bytes by eight. In practice you will also account for headers, TLS overhead, and internal service traffic. A useful example: serving 1 MB photo reads at 10,000 RPS is extreme and would imply tens of gigabits per second. Use CDNs to push static payloads near users and reduce origin bandwidth. The mental checklist is: calculate RPS, estimate payload size after compression, multiply, and convert to the units of the network links you will use. Always sanity-check the result against typical link capacities like 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, or higher. From User Actions to Bandwidth means bandwidth (b/s) = rps × average payload size (bytes). convert to bits/s by ×8 and compare to link capacity.. In practical terms, turn rps and payload sizes into bytes-per-second for network planning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Storage estimation requires separating small, frequent items from large, infrequent ones. User profile records are compact — often a few kilobytes — while media like photos or videos are megabytes each. Multiply item size by item count to estimate raw storage. For example, if each profile is 1 KB and you have 100 million users, that's about 100 GB of raw profile data. Contrast that with photos: if every user uploads 10 photos per year at 2 MB each and there are 100 million users, yearly photo additions are 2,000 TB or about 2 PB. Always include metadata, thumbnails, indexes, and replication factors. If you keep three replicas for durability, multiply your raw totals by three. When raw storage numbers reach hundreds of terabytes or petabytes, a single server or a small cluster is no longer realistic. This forces a move to distributed object storage, sharded databases, or cloud-managed blob stores. The decision threshold depends on durability needs, access patterns, and budget. If reads are frequent for recent items, you might add a cache or a hot store for recent objects and place cold data in cheaper, distributed object storage. Replication and geographic distribution add further costs and complexity but are necessary for availability. For instance, a system with 2 PB of photo uploads per year should architect for multi-node, distributed storage and lifecycle policies like tiering to colder, cheaper storage after 6–12 months. Also plan operational activities: data rebalancing, snapshotting, and backup windows become non-trivial at this scale. Misconceptions include underestimating the operational effort of petabyte-scale storage and assuming simply adding disks to one machine will scale. At scale, consider object stores, erasure coding, and cross-region replication strategies. Latency differences dictate whether you cache, colocate, or accept asynchronous behavior. Here are a set of reference numbers to keep in your head: L1 cache reference is sub-nanosecond; main memory reads are on the order of 100 nanoseconds; compressing 1 KB might take a few microseconds; sending 1 KB over a 1 Gbps link is about 10 microseconds; random 4 KB SSD reads are roughly 150 microseconds; a round trip inside a datacenter is around 500 microseconds; reading 1 MB sequentially from an SSD is about one millisecond; a disk seek is about 10 milliseconds; a round trip between continents can be on the order of 150 milliseconds. These are rules of thumb rather than exact benchmarks, but they show how many orders of magnitude separate memory, storage, and network. Use these numbers to justify cache placement: if a remote call costs 100 ms but memory access is 0.1 µs, caching can reduce user-visible latency by orders of magnitude. A common mistake is treating all input and output as similar; they are not — plan accordingly. Unit conversion errors are one of the most common mistakes during estimation. Always track whether your sizes are in bytes or bits. Network link capacities are often quoted in bits per second (for example, 1 Gbps), while payload sizes are usually measured in bytes. Remember: 1 byte = 8 bits. Also be careful with kilo versus kibibyte conventions; using 1,000 vs 1,024 changes numbers but usually not the order of magnitude. Time units matter too: convert days to seconds (86,400) to compute RPS. Another frequent omission is replication: when you plan for three replicas for durability, multiply raw storage by three. Finally, account for headers, protocol overhead, and non-payload bytes in network calculations. A simple checklist fixes many errors: annotate units next to every number, convert early, round to a comfortable figure, and state replication and compression assumptions. When asked an estimation question in an interview or design meeting, follow a short script: first, state your assumptions clearly — DAU, actions per user, payload sizes, read/write ratio, and peak factor. Second, compute total actions/day and convert to average RPS by dividing by 86,400. Third, apply your peak multiplier and separate reads and writes using your ratio. Fourth, compute storage per data type (profiles, media) and multiply by replication. Fifth, compute bandwidth by multiplying peak RPS by payload size and converting to bits per second. Sixth, use latency reference numbers to justify caching and replication choices. Finally, sanity-check results against typical link sizes and known thresholds: is the resulting bandwidth tens of Mbps, hundreds of Mbps, or hundreds of Gbps? State the implication: CDN necessary, single region sufficient, or multi-region needed. Keep four core ideas in your mental toolbox. First, back-of-the-envelope estimates are about order-of-magnitude correctness, not precise decimals. Second, compute average RPS from DAU and actions/day, then multiply by a peak factor to size capacity. Third, storage estimates must include item size, count, metadata, and replication — media files often drive petabyte-scale needs. Fourth, latency numbers differ by orders of magnitude; use them to justify caches, replication, or asynchronous designs. When you present an estimate, always state assumptions and units.
